title: Wartime Ukraine’s people power protests are Putin’s worst nightmare
gist: The July 15, 2026 dismissal of Ukraine's 35-year-old reformist defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov triggered nationwide protests and the biggest political crisis since the full-scale war began, forcing Zelenskyy to appoint General Mykhailo Drapatyi as new commander in chief. Dickinson argues Ukraine's functioning wartime civil society is precisely what Putin invaded to destroy, which is why he rejects peace deals that would leave a democratic Ukraine standing and why only peace through strength is realistic.

themes.theme: The Fedorov dismissal and the wartime protest wave

insights.claim: Nationwide Ukrainian protests began on July 15 in response to the dismissal of thirty-five-year-old defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov as part of a major government reshuffle, producing the biggest political crisis since the start of the full-scale war.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Domestic political instability in Kyiv is now a live variable for war-effort continuity and for allied confidence in Ukrainian governance.

insights.claim: During six months at the defense ministry Fedorov helped Ukraine regain the battlefield initiative against Russia by enhancing drone warfare capabilities while also moving against deeply entrenched corruption in the defense sector.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Attributes a recent shift in battlefield momentum specifically to drone-capability buildout — a signal for defense-tech and drone supply chains tied to Ukraine.
insights.locator: During his six months at the helm of the defense ministry

insights.claim: Fedorov's reform push brought him into open confrontation with sixty-year-old commander in chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, widely seen as a key member of Ukraine's old guard shaped by Soviet-era thinking, and critics accused Zelenskyy of choosing the past over the future by removing him.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: A generational and doctrinal split inside Ukraine's military leadership — Soviet-era mass warfare versus drone-centric innovation — determines how effectively Western aid converts into battlefield output.
insights.locator: This brought Fedorov into increasingly open confrontation

insights.claim: Within hours of Fedorov's dismissal thousands gathered at makeshift protests in Kyiv and across Ukraine, including large student contingents, military veterans, rights activists, and civic-minded citizens, who stressed they were undeterred by the ever-present threat of Russian bombardment.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Mass street mobilization under active bombardment shows Ukrainian political accountability mechanisms still bind, constraining executive decisions mid-war.
insights.locator: The response to Fedorov’s dismissal was almost immediate

insights.claim: Criticism of the Fedorov removal came from anti-corruption activists, the volunteer community, members of the military, and reportedly from within Zelenskyy's own political party, with many arguing that although unity is vital in wartime they could not remain silent while the fate of the nation was at stake.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Dissent inside the ruling party is the more meaningful signal than street protest for whether Zelenskyy's coalition holds.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Ukrainian society as a whole was actively debating

themes.theme: Zelenskyy's concession and the generational shift

insights.claim: The scale of the public backlash initially took Zelenskyy by surprise, and days after protests broke out he announced popular young general Mykhailo Drapatyi as the new commander in chief of the Ukrainian army, a move widely welcomed as a long-overdue generational shift in military leadership.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: A leadership change at the top of the Ukrainian army driven by street pressure — watch for doctrinal and procurement shifts under Drapatyi.
insights.locator: The scale of the public backlash over the removal of Fedorov

insights.claim: Zelenskyy offered Fedorov several alternative government positions focused on the technological aspects of the war effort, but the former defense minister has rejected them and is insisting on a return to his previous post, leaving the crisis unresolved.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: The standoff is unresolved, so Kyiv political risk has not cleared — further escalation or a reinstatement are both live outcomes.
insights.locator: Zelenskyy has also offered Fedorov a number of potential new positions

insights.claim: Despite the impossibility of holding elections in the current security environment, Ukraine's democratic political culture is clearly intact, as the crisis demonstrated the vibrancy of wartime civil society.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Counters the argument that suspended elections have hollowed out Ukrainian democracy — relevant to Western political support and aid conditionality debates.
insights.locator: It is not yet clear how the political drama in Kyiv will play out

themes.theme: Putin's people-power trauma as causal driver of the war

insights.claim: Putin's fear of people power traces to his Cold War service as a young KGB officer in 1980s East Germany, where he personally witnessed the rapid disintegration of the Soviet Union's European empire as Eastern Bloc populations rose up and turned away from Moscow.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: A biographical model of Putin's decision-making that predicts he treats popular uprisings, not NATO hardware, as the primary threat.
insights.locator: Putin’s fear of people power can be traced back

insights.claim: Putin's efforts to subvert Ukrainian statehood first began to dominate his reign in the aftermath of the 2004 Orange Revolution, a multi-million strong protest movement against a rigged election that marked post-Soviet Ukraine's democratic breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Dates the Russia-Ukraine confrontation to 2004 rather than 2014 or 2022, implying the conflict's driver is regime-security, not any negotiable grievance.
insights.locator: It is no coincidence that the Russian dictator’s efforts

insights.claim: Putin views Ukraine's democracy as a potential catalyst for the next stage in a Russian retreat from empire that began in 1989 with the fall of the Berlin Wall, and has branded Ukraine an artificial 'anti-Russia' that could no longer be tolerated.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Frames the war as imperial-retreat management rather than territorial dispute, which implies no border settlement can end it.

insights.claim: Before resorting to force Putin invested huge sums in pro-Kremlin political parties, business ventures, media outlets, and religious initiatives in Ukraine to weaken the country from within and discredit its European integration, and escalated to military intervention in Crimea and undeclared war in eastern Ukraine in spring 2014 only after that approach backfired and provoked a second people power revolution.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Establishes an escalation ladder — subversion first, force when subversion fails — that is a template for reading Russian behavior in Moldova, Georgia, and the Balkans.
insights.locator: Initially, Putin attempted to subvert Ukrainian independence

insights.claim: For more than two decades Putin has demonstrated a readiness to sacrifice Russia's national interests and international standing in order to prioritize the subjugation of Ukraine, because he believes the consolidation of a democratic, European Ukraine could prove fatal for his own authoritarian empire.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Implies sanctions and economic cost calculations underweight Putin's willingness to absorb damage — a persistent forecasting error in Russia risk pricing.
insights.locator: Today’s war is a continuation of the anti-Ukrainian policies

insights.claim: Despite frequent boasts of his popularity, Putin is aware his grip on power is far less secure than the propaganda machine suggests, which explains his ruthless suppression of all possible domestic opposition.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: If regime insecurity is the real constraint, Russian domestic repression intensity is a better leading indicator of policy than approval polling.

themes.theme: Why negotiated peace fails and what follows

insights.claim: Putin has rejected a number of peace proposals that would end the invasion while securing Russia's territorial gains, because any compromise deal would oblige him to accept an independent and democratic Ukraine on Russia's border — seen in Moscow as a defeat of historic proportions.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Territorially generous ceasefire proposals will keep failing; do not price near-term peace-deal optionality into Russia/Ukraine-exposed assets.
insights.quote: While such terms may at first glance appear generous, any compromise peace deal would also oblige Putin to accept the geopolitical reality of an independent and democratic Ukraine on Russia’s border.
insights.locator: The recent wave of protests in Ukraine would be unthinkable

insights.claim: The only realistic option for Ukraine and its allies is to pursue peace through strength, because seeking a negotiated settlement with Putin is futile.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Argues for sustained defense-spending and armament flows rather than diplomatic off-ramps — supportive of a multi-year European defense procurement cycle.
insights.quote: It is therefore futile to seek some kind of negotiated settlement with Putin.

insights.claim: Ukrainian democracy remains blighted by a lack of ideological principles that reduces elections to popularity contests, along with oligarch interference and endemic corruption, yet the population's ability to influence its political classes is undeniable and terrifies the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: A candid acknowledgment of Ukrainian governance flaws that will shape EU accession and reconstruction-fund conditionality.
insights.locator: Ukrainian democracy is far from perfect

insights.claim: The recent wave of protests in Ukraine would be unthinkable in today's Russia, but Putin remains fearful that Ukrainian courage could eventually prove contagious.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Contagion fear, not territory, is the war's driver — meaning Russian escalation risk persists even after battlefield lines freeze.
